observation: McCrudden & Schraw's goal-focusing model and follow-up studies found readers given explicit purpose/relevance instructions recalled more purpose-relevant material than non-relevant text, reading relevant segments no slower than readers without instructions.
claim: A stated or inferred reading purpose changes selectivity of encoding (what gets remembered), not just time-on-task; L0/L1 content generation should be conditionable on a small, closed purpose taxonomy (studying, deciding, replying, browsing) rather than open-ended free text.
mechanism: Relevance instructions narrow processing goals, which guide attention allocation and memory without costing reading speed.
population: general students/adults (multi-study lab program from one research lab)

implications.text: Infer purpose from context (calendar proximity, document source) into 3-5 closed categories, surfaced as a low-friction correctable chip rather than an upfront free-text question.

observation: Hulleman & Harackiewicz (2009, Science) and Harackiewicz et al. (2016) found students who write in their own words how material connects to their life show higher interest and better outcomes than a control, with the largest gains for low-expectancy students; Canning & Harackiewicz's companion line of work found directly telling a low-confidence student why material is useful can backfire and reduce interest versus no message at all.
claim: Riemann should never auto-assert personal relevance ('this matters for your ECE4078 lab because...') as system-generated text; instead offer an optional one-tap prompt for the user's own self-generated relevance statement.
mechanism: Self-generated relevance connections carry the utility-value benefit; system-told relevance claims can be read as presumptuous or as an unfavorable signal by exactly the users who would benefit most, inverting the effect.
population: general students, especially low-expectancy learners (multiple field RCTs in real classrooms)

implications.text: Offer an optional one-tap 'why does this matter to you?' prompt whose answer is Sam's own words, rather than generating an asserted relevance line on his behalf.

observation: Delgado, Vargas, Ackerman & Salmerón (2018, meta-analysis of 54 studies, >170,000 participants) and Clinton (2019, independent meta-analysis) both found a screen-reading disadvantage concentrated in expository text (g≈-0.21 to -0.27), absent for narrative text, and apparently growing rather than shrinking in more recent studies; screen readers also show worse-calibrated metacomprehension (overconfidence) than paper readers.
claim: Riemann's core content (expository documents) sits in exactly the regime where screen-reading disadvantage is largest, and this should be treated as a real headwind the design must actively counter through structure (L0/L1 orientation, paging), not assumed away by using a screen at all.
mechanism: The screen disadvantage for expository text is a replicated, converging effect across two independent large meta-analyses, distinct from the narrative-text case where no disadvantage exists.
population: general adult readers (two independent large meta-analyses)

implications.text: Lean harder on structural mitigations (L0/L1 orientation, discrete paging) to counter the expository-text screen disadvantage, rather than assuming a well-designed screen reader is exempt from it.

observation: Sun, Shen & Chen (n=140) found that under time pressure, screen readers' comprehension dropped further relative to print, and mind-wandering probes showed print readers successfully suppressed task-unrelated thought under pressure while screen readers did not.
claim: Adding time pressure (e.g. a countdown) to screen-based reading may actively worsen comprehension rather than help it, directly undercutting the intuitive 'give people a time budget to force focus' design instinct.
mechanism: Screen reading under pressure appears to be an attention-control failure — screen readers fail to suppress mind-wandering when demands increase, where paper readers succeed.
population: general adult readers (single well-designed study, n=140, not yet independently replicated)
context: lab, reading medium x time pressure design

implications.text: Do not add a countdown/time-pressure mechanic on the assumption it will improve focus; test any deadline-proximity UI change carefully rather than defaulting to a countdown.

observation: Paging (fixed, spatially stable pages) produces more coherent recall/summaries and more strategic backtracking than continuous scrolling across several studies; the cost of continuous scrolling is worse for readers lower in working-memory capacity.
claim: The zoom dial should feel like discrete, spatially stable 'pages' per level rather than continuous scroll, especially valuable given ADHD-linked working-memory variability.
mechanism: Scrolled text lacks a stable spatial 'place' for content, forcing readers to hold content in memory rather than using positional memory the way paged/paper reading allows.
population: general adult readers, effect stronger for lower-working-memory-capacity readers
context: multiple converging older and newer studies, no large meta-analysis

implications.text: Design the zoom dial's content presentation as discrete, spatially stable pages per level, not a continuously scrolling surface.

observation: A 1980 meta-analysis of 135 studies (Ausubel's advance-organizer research) establishes a consistent facilitative effect of previewing structure before detail on comprehension and retention, moderated by reader ability; the conclusion-first/BLUF/inverted-pyramid convention itself is a journalism/writing craft convention, not directly tested as a reading-comprehension RCT manipulation.
claim: Riemann's fixed gist-before-detail zoom order (L0→L1→L2→L3) is well supported by advance-organizer research independent of purpose-conditioning, and should remain the always-on default scaffold, with purpose-conditioning layered on top (reweighting which sections surface) rather than replacing the coarse-to-fine order.
mechanism: Orienting structure before detail is a long-replicated facilitative effect; conclusion-first ordering specifically is an adjacent, well-motivated but not directly RCT-tested convention.
population: general students, mostly classroom-based (45-year-old base meta-analysis, not digital-reading-specific)
context: classroom-based, long-replicated across decades of follow-up

implications.text: Keep the L0→L1→L2→L3 gist-first order as the always-on default; use purpose-conditioning to reweight which sections surface at L1/L2, not to override the coarse-to-fine order itself.

observation: Ramirez & Beilock (2011, Science, two studies including a real high-school classroom final exam) found 10 minutes of expressive writing about test-related worry before a stressful exam improved scores, largest for habitually test-anxious students; brief (~15-minute) single-session mindfulness inductions for working memory show genuinely mixed results in the literature, and no source tests anything as brief as a one-line grounding phrase.
claim: A one-line grounding phrase before reading is a plausible, near-zero-cost UI nicety, but is 1-2 orders of magnitude smaller than the actual doses (10-minute writing, 15-minute breathing) shown to work — it should be shipped as optional and skippable, never oversold internally as an evidence-based intervention.
mechanism: The Ramirez & Beilock mechanism (worry competes with working memory, so offloading it frees capacity) is theoretically compatible with a much smaller version, but the evidenced dose is far larger than a single line of copy.
population: general students, test-anxious students showing largest gains (real classroom RCT)
context: lab and real classroom-exam RCT; scope is pre-exam anxiety specifically, not general brief grounding

implications.text: Ship any grounding phrase as optional, skippable, near-zero-cost UI copy, explicitly not claimed as an evidence-based intervention given the dose mismatch with the supporting studies.
